text: It's tempting to measure a platform the way you'd measure any production system: is it up, is it fast, are there incidents. Those numbers matter, but they answer a different question than the one that actually determines whether the platform is doing its job. This lesson covers the metrics that answer the question that matters — whether it's genuinely reducing cognitive load, not just whether it stays running.

A platform can have excellent uptime and still be failing, if teams have quietly stopped routing real work through it. Uptime measures reliability. It says nothing about whether anyone is choosing to use the thing, or how much friction remains in using it well. That gap is exactly why this chapter needs a second category of metric, one closer to Lesson 1's actual promise of absorbing cognitive load.

Developer onboarding time — how long until a new hire ships a first real contribution — is a direct read on whether that promise is being kept. Time-to-first-deploy narrows it further: the elapsed time from starting a brand-new service to its first successful production deployment. Both are sensitive to exactly the friction a golden path should remove, and a platform that's genuinely working should make both numbers shrink predictably over time.

Golden-path adoption rate is the metric most directly tied to Lesson 2's warning: the share of services actually built the supported way, versus the share that went around it. A low adoption rate, even when the path is technically available to everyone, is a direct signal that it doesn't fit real needs yet or isn't trusted — not a vanity number to improve for its own sake. Pair that with deliberately measured developer satisfaction, because silence isn't the same as satisfaction; teams that have quietly built workarounds rarely file a complaint about it.

None of these numbers exist to decorate a quarterly review. A platform run as a product uses them the way an external product team uses usage data: a spike in time-to-first-deploy points straight at a bottleneck worth fixing, and a golden path with low adoption needs real investigation, not a louder mandate. That's the payoff of this whole chapter — a platform stops being infrastructure you hope is helping, and becomes a product whose impact you can actually see and keep improving.
